title: Focus on products
blurb: Explain why PRINCE2 defines and agrees products and their quality before doing the work, and how product descriptions drive the project.
question: A team starts building a new booking system before anyone has agreed what it must do or how it will be judged acceptable. Which principle is being neglected?

teach.body: Formally: a PRINCE2 project focuses on the definition and delivery of products, in particular their user quality expectations and requirements. In plain English: agree exactly what is to be delivered, and what 'good enough' means for each item, before working out the tasks. PRINCE2 calls these outputs 'products', and a project is output-oriented, not work-oriented.

rows.label: Scope control
values: No more work than the products need

teach.h: What a product description sets out
head: Heading
Answers the question
rows: What parts does it consist of?
How good must it be, and how is that checked?
Who checks it and who approves it?
teach.caption: Product descriptions give everyone the same clear picture of each product.
Only then are work packages, estimates and the schedule built. This is product-based planning.

teach.h: One idea that drives four practices
teach.body: Product focus is the basis of planning (product-based planning), quality (quality specifications in each product description), scope (the products in a plan) and change control (changes are judged against agreed, baselined products). It also controls scope creep: the project does no more work than needed to deliver its agreed products. Co-creating products with business, user and supplier communities improves adoption and reduces handover risks.

steps.label: Output
steps.sub: the product delivered: a new app

steps.label: Outcome
steps.sub: the result of change: customers book online

teach.caption: Focus on products is about outputs and their quality. Outcomes and benefits belong to the business case.

teach.body: Linwood Water wants an app for reporting leaks. Before any coding, project manager Deepa Nair works with senior user Owen Price to write the project product description, including the acceptance criterion that a report can be sent in under two minutes. Each product (the app, the map layer, the staff guide) gets a product description with quality specifications. When a director asks for a billing feature, Deepa checks it against the agreed products and raises it as a request for change rather than slipping it in.

teach.text: Classic traps: (1) Defining WHAT is in scope is focus on products; the RANGE scope may vary within (scope tolerance) is manage by exception. (2) An outcome or a benefit is not a product. (3) Product descriptions are written for products at every level of plan, not only for the final product.

items: Define and deliver products, with their user quality expectations and requirements.
Output-oriented, not work-oriented: no more work than needed for the agreed products.
Product descriptions: purpose, composition, derivation, format, quality specifications and method.
Products drive planning, quality, scope and change control.

summary: You can now explain the focus on products principle, list what a product description defines, and show how agreed products drive planning, quality, scope and change control. You can also separate it from manage by exception's scope tolerance.

A.q: Which statement describes the focus on products principle?
options: Tasks are scheduled before outputs are agreed
Products and their quality are defined and delivered
Benefits are measured at each stage boundary
Products are approved by the business layer
A.why: A PRINCE2 project focuses on the definition and delivery of products, in particular their user quality expectations and requirements (manual 2.6).

whyNot.0: This is the work-oriented approach PRINCE2 avoids; products are defined first.
whyNot.2: Measuring benefits relates to the business case and business justification.
whyNot.3: Products are approved by those named in their product descriptions, within the project.

A.q: What does PRINCE2 mean by a project being 'output-oriented'?
options: It reports progress by hours worked
It focuses on business outcomes
It is organized around its products
It measures benefits during delivery
A.why: Projects should be output-oriented, not work-oriented: they are organized around the products (outputs) they deliver.

whyNot.1: Outcomes are results of change; products are the outputs that enable them.
whyNot.3: Measuring benefits belongs to the business case practice.

A.q: Which product sets out a product's purpose, composition, derivation, format and quality specifications?
options: Work package description
Product breakdown structure
Quality register
Product description
A.why: The product description defines each product's purpose, composition, derivation, format, quality specifications and quality method.

whyNot.0: A work package description passes responsibility for producing products to a team.
whyNot.1: A product breakdown structure is a hierarchy of all a plan's products.
whyNot.2: The quality register records quality activities and their results.

B.q:
Which two statements about focus on products are correct?
1. It helps control scope creep.
2. It is the basis of product-based planning.
3. It is applied only to the project's final product.
4. It requires products to be built before they are described.
options: 1 and 3
2 and 4
3 and 4
1 and 2
B.why: Doing no more work than needed for agreed products controls scope creep (1), and product focus is the basis of product-based planning (2).

whyNot.0: Statement 3 is false: product descriptions cover products at every level of plan.
whyNot.1: Statement 4 is false: products are defined before they are built.
whyNot.2: Both are false: product focus covers all levels of plan, and products are described before they are built.

B.q: A sponsor asks for an extra feature that is not in the agreed product descriptions. How does focus on products help?
options: It lets the change be judged against agreed products
It lets the team add the feature within tolerance
It moves the decision to the business layer
It records the feature as a project risk
B.why: Product focus underpins change control: a request is assessed against the agreed, baselined products.

whyNot.1: Adding unagreed work is scope creep; it needs change control.
whyNot.2: Requests for change are decided within the project, by the board or a change authority.
whyNot.3: A request for change is an issue, not a risk.

B.q: Which is an example of a product rather than an outcome or a benefit?
options: Staff use the new system every day
A 15% fall in processing costs
Faster responses to customers
A printed staff user guide
B.why: A user guide is an output, a product the project delivers.

whyNot.0: Changed behaviour is an outcome: a result of change.
whyNot.1: A measurable improvement is a benefit.
whyNot.2: Faster responses describe an outcome of using the products.

C.q: Which process creates the project product description, and what does it include?
options: Starting up a project; the user's quality expectations
Initiating a project; the product flow diagram
Managing product delivery; the work package tolerances
Starting up a project; the detailed stage schedule
C.why: The project product description is created in starting up a project and includes the user's quality expectations and acceptance criteria.

whyNot.1: The project product description is created in starting up, not initiation, and a product flow diagram is a separate planning product.
whyNot.2: Managing product delivery is the team manager's process; tolerances are in the work package description.
whyNot.3: Starting up is the right process, but a project product description holds no schedule; schedules belong in plans.

C.q: Which principle is applied by defining scope tolerance, and which by defining what is in scope?
options: Manage by stages; focus on products
Manage by exception; focus on products
Focus on products; manage by exception
Focus on products; manage by stages
C.why: Scope tolerance (how far scope may vary) is manage by exception; defining what is in scope through products and product descriptions is focus on products.

whyNot.0: Manage by stages is about stage-by-stage planning and decisions, not scope tolerance.
whyNot.3: Manage by stages does not define what is in scope.

C.q: Why does PRINCE2 encourage co-creating products with business, user and supplier communities?
options: It removes the need for product descriptions
It moves product approval to the users
It improves adoption and reduces handover risk
It lets the supplier set the quality criteria
C.why: Co-creating products with agreed product descriptions unites perspectives, improves adoption and reduces handover risks (manual 3.5.1).

whyNot.0: Co-creation works with agreed product descriptions, not instead of them.
whyNot.1: Approval follows the product description; co-creation does not change who approves.
whyNot.3: Quality expectations come from users; co-creation unites all perspectives.

reteach.title: Ordering a cake, not hiring a baker by the hour
reteach.question: You order a birthday cake. Do you describe the hours of baking you want, or the cake?

blocks.body: You describe the cake: size, flavour, decoration, when you need it, and how you will judge it (it must feed 20 and be nut-free). The baker then works out the tasks. If you later want a second tier, that is a change you agree, not something that just appears on the bill. PRINCE2 works the same way: products and their quality are agreed in product descriptions first, and the work follows from them.

blocks.text: The party going well is the outcome; the cake is the product.

explain.body: The principle is about defining and delivering products, especially their user quality expectations and requirements.

test.q: What does focus on products particularly emphasize about each product?
options: Its user quality expectations and requirements
Its cost compared with the project budget
Its place in the business layer's portfolio
Its supplier's contract and payment terms
test.why: The principle focuses on products, in particular their user quality expectations and requirements.

whyNot.1: Cost belongs to plans and tolerances rather than this principle's emphasis.
whyNot.2: Portfolio position is a business layer concern.
whyNot.3: Contracts are handled through the commercial management approach.

explain.body: Each product description sets out purpose, composition, derivation, format, quality specifications and quality method, and who reviews and approves the product.

test.q: Which is a heading you would expect in a product description?
options: Composition
Tolerances
Stage plan
Lessons
test.why: Composition (what the product consists of) is a product description heading, with purpose, derivation, format and quality specifications.

whyNot.1: Tolerances sit in plans and work package descriptions.
whyNot.2: A stage plan is a separate management product.
whyNot.3: Lessons are held in the lessons log and lessons report.

explain.body: Because the project is output-oriented, it does only the work needed to deliver its agreed products, which controls scope creep.

test.q: How does focus on products help prevent scope creep?
options: By widening scope tolerance
By linking work to agreed products
By shortening each stage
By escalating every change
test.why: The project does no more work than is needed to deliver its agreed products.

whyNot.0: Scope tolerance is set under manage by exception and widening it would allow more variation.
whyNot.2: Stage length is a manage by stages decision.
whyNot.3: Changes are assessed through change control; not every change is escalated.

explain.body: Products underpin planning (product-based planning), quality (specifications), scope (a plan's products) and change control (changes against baselined products).

test.q: Which planning technique is a direct application of focus on products?
options: Critical path analysis
Exception management
Product-based planning
Risk budgeting
test.why: Product-based planning starts by defining products, then derives work, estimates and schedule from them.

whyNot.0: Critical path analysis is a scheduling technique, not based on defining products first.
whyNot.1: Exception management applies manage by exception.
whyNot.3: A risk budget funds risk responses; it is not a product-focused technique.
